subcategory: Terminal Units, Pumps, and the Scope Boundary
questionText: A glycol rooftop loop needs fluid every month. The professional response is:

choices.text: Find and repair the leak, then restore the correct glycol percentage verified by refractometer
Switch to plain water in summer

explanation: Recurring loss = leak, and water top-offs silently dilute freeze protection toward a burst coil. Fix the leak; verify the mix.

questionText: Large buildings distribute cooling as chilled water because:

choices.text: Water carries vastly more heat per volume than air, shrinking distribution to pipes

explanation: Thousands of times the heat capacity per volume: pipes replace hallway-sized ducts.

questionText: Typical chilled water design temperatures are:
explanation: The classic 44/54 with a 10°F design delta — the numbers coil diagnosis is read against.

questionText: A cooling tower rejects heat primarily by:

choices.text: Evaporation of a portion of the condenser water

explanation: Latent heat of evaporation does the work — which ties tower capacity to ambient wet bulb.

questionText: Tower APPROACH is:

choices.text: The water temperature drop across the tower
How close leaving water gets to ambient wet-bulb temperature

explanation: Approach measures tower effectiveness; range measures the drop. A widening approach = a sick tower.

questionText: Neglected cooling towers are a life-safety issue because of:
explanation: Warm aerated water + neglect = Legionella habitat; treatment and cleaning are mandatory, documented duties.

questionText: Condensing boilers achieve their rated efficiency only when:

choices.text: Return water is cool enough (≲130°F) for flue gas to condense — hence outdoor reset

explanation: No condensation, no latent recovery: cool return water is the whole trick, and reset controls provide it.

questionText: A relief valve that weeps each heating cycle with pressure climbing sharply indicates:

choices.text: A waterlogged expansion tank (or failed fill valve) — never plug the relief

explanation: Expansion with nowhere to go becomes overpressure; the relief is the witness and must stay in service.

questionText: Hydronic loop fill pressure must account for:

choices.text: Building height — about 1 psi per 2.3 feet plus margin, or upper floors air-bind

explanation: Static height sets minimum pressure; low fill = cold, gurgling top floors.

questionText: A clogged strainer in a hydronic loop presents as:

choices.text: Pressure drop across it and starved flow downstream — the water-side dirty filter

explanation: Strainers protect coils and pumps and clog like filters; gauge pressure across them tells the story.

questionText: Entry-level hydronic scope typically excludes:

choices.text: Chiller refrigerant-circuit internals, steam boiler work, and large burner management — licensed/factory territory

explanation: Diagnose to the boundary, document, refer — the kettle/suppression rule at plant scale.

questionText: A conference room turns drowsy in every long meeting; CO2 logs to 1,600 ppm while the DCV damper never moves. The likely fault is:

choices.text: The CO2 sensor (drifted/failed) never reporting occupancy, so demand-controlled ventilation never opens

explanation: DCV can only respond to what its sensor reports. A drifted sensor starves the full room — calibrate/replace, then verify damper response.

questionText: An ERV differs from an HRV because the ERV:

choices.text: Exchanges moisture as well as heat between exhaust and intake air

explanation: The E is enthalpy: ERVs transfer latent (moisture) plus sensible energy — the humid-climate choice, per Module 13's latent lesson.

questionText: A dental office upgraded to MERV 13 filters in the same 1-inch slots; two weeks later coils are freezing and the blower is loud. The engineering error was:

choices.text: Ignoring the static-pressure budget — high-MERV needs more media area (deep cabinets), not denser 1-inch filters

explanation: Module 14 again: efficiency costs static. Deep-pleat media cabinets buy the pressure back; dense 1-inch filters strangle the system.

questionText: A restaurant's dining room doors whistle inward and outside odors ride in; the kitchen exhaust runs full tilt with a failed make-up air unit. The building is:

choices.text: Negatively pressurized — exhaust exceeds supply, and the envelope is making up the difference

explanation: The exhaust/supply ledger is unbalanced; every crack becomes an intake. Restore make-up air and the doors go quiet — the cross-trade classic.

questionText: ASHRAE 62.1 governs:

choices.text: Minimum outdoor-air ventilation rates for occupied buildings

explanation: The ventilation standard: outdoor air per person and per floor area, delivered and verifiable.

questionText: Indoor CO2 near 1,500 ppm in an occupied room indicates:
explanation: CO2 proxies ventilation adequacy: outdoor ~420 ppm; sustained >1,000-1,100 ppm means the room is starved of outdoor air.

questionText: Demand-controlled ventilation modulates outdoor air based on:
explanation: DCV matches ventilation to actual occupancy — and inherits every fault of its CO2 sensors.

questionText: An ERV transfers ______ between exhaust and intake:
explanation: Enthalpy recovery: sensible + latent, cutting the cost of conditioning ventilation air, especially in humid climates.

questionText: Ventilation intakes must be located:

choices.text: Near exhaust outlets for short ducts
Away from exhausts, flues, and loading docks — or the building re-inhales contamination

explanation: Walk the outside: intake placement is the most literal IAQ diagnosis there is.

questionText: Sustained indoor RH above about 60% risks:

choices.text: Mold growth and dust mite proliferation

explanation: Humidity is mold's enabler; the 30-60% band is the comfort AND health target.

questionText: The honest way to deliver a MERV 13 upgrade is:

choices.text: Media-area engineering: deep-pleat cabinets sized to the system's static budget

explanation: Filtration efficiency costs static; surface area pays the bill without strangling airflow.

questionText: Commercial buildings are usually designed to run:

choices.text: Slightly positive so conditioned air leaks out and unfiltered air stays out

explanation: Slight positive pressure keeps the envelope defending itself; negative buildings inhale their problems.

questionText: A negatively pressurized building announces itself by:

choices.text: Whistling entries, doors that fight you, drafts, and backdrafting flues

explanation: The envelope becomes the make-up air path — audible, tangible, and dangerous around combustion.

questionText: The building-pressure diagnosis ledger compares:

choices.text: Everything exhausting air vs everything supplying it (plus stack effect)

explanation: Hoods, dryers, and exhaust fans against OA dampers and make-up units: balance the ledger, cure the building.

questionText: The condenser will not run. At the air handler, R-to-C reads 26VAC and Y-to-C reads 26VAC with cooling called. At the condenser, Y-to-C reads 0V. The fault is:

choices.text: The Y conductor between air handler and condenser (or its splices) — the call is leaving but not arriving

explanation: The command exists at the source and is absent at the destination: the wire path between them (weather-exposed and chafed at the condenser entry, classically) is the suspect.

questionText: A board's 3A control fuse blows the moment the thermostat calls cooling. The professional next step is:

choices.text: Hunt the short on the Y circuit — chafed stat wire or a shorted contactor coil — before any new fuse

explanation: The fuse is doing its job against a real short that appears when Y energizes. Bigger fuses convert a protected fault into a burned transformer or board.

questionText: A house is always too cold in the evening although equipment tests perfectly. The thermostat wall gets blasted by a west-facing sunset window. The mechanism is:

choices.text: The stat senses the sun-heated wall as room temperature and over-cools the actual space

explanation: The system serves whatever its sensor experiences. A lying location produces faithful equipment executing bad orders — relocate or shade the sensor.

subcategory: Sequences of Operation and Smart Thermostats
questionText: After a power blink, a homeowner reports their AC "takes five minutes to come back and must be broken." The explanation is:

choices.text: The compressor short-cycle protection timer — a designed delay that protects against restarting into high head pressure

explanation: Anti-short-cycle timers are universal protection. Recognizing designed delays prevents replacing healthy parts for correct behavior.

subcategory: Sequences of Operation and Smart Thermostats
questionText: A newly installed smart thermostat without a C wire causes the furnace blower to pulse briefly at random. The mechanism is:

choices.text: Power-stealing: the stat sips current through equipment circuits, occasionally enough to twitch relays

explanation: Without a common, the stat powers itself through the call wires — the phantom-cycling signature. Pull a C wire or fit the add-a-wire kit.

questionText: In the 24V alphabet, energizing R-to-Y-to-G produces:

choices.text: Cooling: condenser contactor plus indoor blower

explanation: Y pulls the outdoor contactor, G runs the blower — the standard cooling call.

questionText: The C terminal provides:

choices.text: The 24V common return path — required by smart thermostats

explanation: C completes the control circuit; power-stealing stats without it flicker and phantom-cycle.

questionText: Transformer health is verified by measuring:
explanation: Hot-to-common shows the control supply; everything else is switching downstream of it.

questionText: 24V measured ACROSS a supposedly closed safety switch means:

choices.text: It is actually open — dropping the full control voltage

explanation: Voltage-drop logic at control scale: closed contacts read ~0V across; the full 24V appears across the open point.

questionText: A repeatedly blowing 3A board fuse demands:

choices.text: Finding the control-circuit short (chafed wires, shorted coils) before re-fusing

explanation: The fuse protects the transformer and board from a real short; upsizing it relocates the burning.

questionText: The O terminal on most heat pump brands:

choices.text: Energizes the reversing valve in COOLING

explanation: O = energized in cooling (B = heating on some brands) — mis-set O/B makes systems heat when cooling is called.

questionText: A sequence of operation is used diagnostically by:

choices.text: Finding the first step where observed behavior diverges from the written sequence

explanation: The sequence is the map; the divergence point localizes the fault to a testable step.

questionText: The 5-minute compressor delay after power interruption exists to:

choices.text: Prevent restarting against unequalized head pressure
Let refrigerant settle into the compressor

explanation: Starting into high head stalls and damages compressors; the timer lets pressures equalize.

questionText: A mis-configured smart thermostat (wrong O/B, wrong stage timing) presents as:

choices.text: Convincing hardware faults — verify configuration with the same rigor as wiring

explanation: Configuration is the software wiring; the kitchen course's mis-config lesson applies to stats verbatim.

questionText: Comfort complaints that defy equipment diagnosis warrant:

choices.text: Evaluating the thermostat's location and what its wall actually experiences

explanation: The system obeys its sensor. Sun, lamps, drafts, and hollow cold walls make honest equipment misbehave.

questionText: The BAS graphic shows a VAV damper commanded to 85% with normal airflow expected, but the room is stuffy and a flow hood shows almost no supply air. The next move is:

choices.text: Physically inspect the box: verify the actuator actually drives the damper to 85% — command vs reality is the diagnosis

explanation: Graphics report commands and feedback, not truth. A stripped actuator coupling shows perfect on screen and motionless in the duct.

questionText: An AHU has behaved strangely for months; you find its supply fan point set to "hand" at 60% from some forgotten past service call. The lesson is:

choices.text: Check for overrides early — a point in hand ignores all logic and imitates every possible fault

explanation: Overrides outlive their reasons. The override check is the BAS equivalent of checking whether the breaker is on.

questionText: A supply-fan VFD runs at 100% and the ductwork howls; the BAS shows duct static reading 0.1 in. w.c. against a 1.5 setpoint, but a manometer at the sensor tap reads 1.6. The fault is:

choices.text: The duct static-pressure sensor/transmitter lying low — the drive is faithfully chasing a false reading

explanation: The drive obeys its reference. A dead/drifted static sensor reads starved, so the loop floors the fan — verify the sensor before the drive, always.

questionText: Before megger-testing a motor served by a VFD you must:

choices.text: Disconnect the motor leads from the drive — megger voltage destroys the drive's IGBTs

explanation: Insulation-test voltage into the drive's output stage kills it. Isolate the motor first; verify the bus is discharged besides.

questionText: A fan slowed to 50% speed draws approximately what fraction of full-speed power?

choices.text: About 12-13% — power scales with the cube of speed

explanation: 0.5³ = 0.125. The affinity-law cube is the entire economic argument for variable speed.

questionText: DDC stands for:

choices.text: Direct digital control — networked controllers running programmed logic

explanation: Digital controllers replace thermostat switching with programmed, networked logic.

questionText: The dominant open protocol in building automation is:
explanation: BACnet dominates open BAS networking, with Modbus common at equipment interfaces.

questionText: BAS graphics should be treated as:

choices.text: What the system thinks — always verifiable against physical reality

explanation: Command and feedback are not the same as motion and flow: verify at the equipment.

questionText: A point left in "hand"/override:

choices.text: Ignores all programmed logic — a classic source of long-standing mystery behavior

explanation: Overrides outlive their reasons; checking for them is step one on any BAS-served equipment.

questionText: A drifted space temperature sensor on a VAV box causes:

choices.text: The box faithfully serving a false temperature — freezing or cooking the room

explanation: The kitchen probe lesson at building scale: controls are only as honest as their sensors.

questionText: A VFD produces variable speed by:

choices.text: Rectifying to a DC bus and inverting to variable-frequency AC through IGBTs

explanation: Rectifier → DC bus → IGBT inverter — the UPS architecture driving a motor.

questionText: Fan affinity laws mean a fan at 80% speed draws about:

choices.text: Half the power — power scales with speed cubed

explanation: 0.8³ ≈ 0.51: the cube law is the VFD energy story.

questionText: A VFD overvoltage fault during deceleration usually indicates:

choices.text: Decel ramp too fast — the motor regenerates into the DC bus

explanation: A spinning load driven to slow quickly becomes a generator; longer decel or braking options absorb it.

questionText: VFD DC bus capacitors demand:

choices.text: UPS-style discharge verification before touching — they hold lethal charge after power-off

explanation: The same capacitor discipline as UPS work: verify discharge per manual and meter.

questionText: A drive-served fan stuck at max with howling ducts is investigated first at:

choices.text: The speed reference — commonly a failed duct static-pressure sensor

explanation: The drive obeys its reference; a lying static sensor floors the loop. Inputs before electronics — always.

questionText: A 2009 R-22 condenser needs a $1,400 compressor plus refrigerant at scarcity prices. The professional framing is:

choices.text: Just repair it — R-22 is still legal to use
Present repair vs replacement honestly: legal-but-scarce refrigerant, unit age, and the economics of investing in a dead platform
Retrofit it to R-410A by swapping gas

explanation: Serving R-22 systems is legal with recovered supply, but big repairs on the dead platform demand the honest numbers conversation. Drop-in gas swaps between pressure classes are not a thing.

questionText: The practical meaning of the A2L classification is:

choices.text: Mildly flammable: hard to ignite and slow-burning, but demanding rated equipment, no ignition sources, and sensor/ventilation discipline

explanation: 2L = lower flammability. Not propane (A3), but real enough to change tools, cylinders, and work habits.

questionText: You connect gauges to an unlabeled system and the pressures make no sense against any single PT chart. A previous tech may have topped off with a different refrigerant. The correct action is:

choices.text: Treat the charge as contaminated: recover it into a dedicated cylinder for reclaim/destruction, evacuate, and recharge with the correct single refrigerant
Add more of whichever is cheaper

explanation: Mixed refrigerants have no valid PT chart and cannot be serviced. Recover as contaminated (never vent), then rebuild the charge properly.

questionText: Six months after another company's compressor swap, the TXV sticks and the new liquid-line drier shows a temperature drop. Opening the line set reveals black flakes. The root cause was:

choices.text: Brazing without flowing nitrogen — oxide scale from the repair now circulates through the circuit

explanation: Open-air brazing lines the tubing with cupric-oxide scale that the refrigerant then harvests into valves and driers. The nitrogen purge habit exists to prevent exactly this cascade.

questionText: A heat pump's crankcase heater failed in November. The winter risk is:

choices.text: Refrigerant migrating into cold compressor oil between cycles, then a slugging, oil-washed start

explanation: Refrigerant migrates to the coldest point — an off compressor — and dissolves into the oil. The next start pumps foam and liquid: the crankcase heater is compressor life insurance.

questionText: R-22 today is:

choices.text: Production-banned — legacy systems run on recovered/reclaimed supply at scarcity prices

explanation: The phase-out reframes major R-22 repairs as replacement conversations.

questionText: R-410A relative to R-22 operates at:

choices.text: Substantially higher pressures, requiring rated gauges and components

explanation: Roughly 50-70% higher pressures — hardware and habits must be rated for it.

questionText: The A2L classification of R-454B and R-32 means:

choices.text: Mildly flammable — rated tools, leak sensors, no ignition sources, ventilation awareness

explanation: Lower-flammability class: hard to ignite, but it changes cylinders, machines, and work practice.

questionText: Mixed/unknown refrigerant in a system must be:

choices.text: Topped off with the majority component
Recovered as contaminated for reclaim/destruction, then the system evacuated and recharged correctly

explanation: Blends have no PT chart and cannot be serviced; venting remains illegal regardless.

questionText: The correct charge method for a from-empty TXV split system is:

choices.text: Charge to a clear sight glass
Weigh in nameplate charge plus line-set adders, then verify subcooling

explanation: Weight sets the charge; subcooling verifies it — with airflow confirmed before either.

questionText: Brazing refrigerant lines requires nitrogen flowing because:

choices.text: It prevents internal oxide scale that later plugs TXVs and driers

explanation: Open-air brazing scale is the hidden killer of valves downstream — the cheapest prevention in the trade.

questionText: Any time a sealed system is opened, the filter-drier is:

choices.text: Replaced — driers are one-use moisture/debris sponges

explanation: A loaded drier protects nothing; replacement is standard practice on every opening.

questionText: A heat pump accumulator exists to:

choices.text: Catch liquid refrigerant from the winter evaporator before it slugs the compressor

explanation: Cold-weather evaporators can send liquid down the suction line; the accumulator intercepts it.

questionText: Bubbles in a liquid-line sight glass indicate:

choices.text: Flash gas from undercharge or upstream restriction — verify with subcooling

explanation: Flash gas means incomplete condensation or pressure loss; subcooling numbers settle which.

questionText: The professional response to "just top it off like every spring" is:

choices.text: Leak detection, repair, proof (pressure/vacuum hold), and documentation — a leaking system is not a service plan

explanation: Recurring gas loss is a leak: fixing it is the repair; renting refrigerant by installment is not.

questionText: During a spring PM, the dual run capacitor measures 38µF on a 45µF ±6% rating. The unit runs fine today. The professional move is:

choices.text: Document the out-of-tolerance reading and recommend replacement now, before the July failure it predicts
Replace it silently and bill later

explanation: A capacitor 15% under rating in April is a heat-wave failure in waiting. Catching drift is the entire point of measured, recorded PM.

questionText: The reason PM visits record amps, splits, and capacitor values rather than just checking them is:

choices.text: Year-over-year comparison reveals drift long before failure — the baseline habit annualized

explanation: A single reading says "okay today"; a trend says "failing by August." Recorded baselines convert PM from inspection to prediction.

subcategory: The Heating-Season PM and the Agreement Business
questionText: The single highest-value proactive act on a fall furnace PM is:

choices.text: Cleaning the flame sensor and verifying the microamp signal — preventing the classic mid-winter lockout

explanation: The oxidized flame rod is the most common winter no-heat. Thirty seconds of abrasive cloth in October prevents the emergency call in January.

subcategory: The Heating-Season PM and the Agreement Business
questionText: A fall heat pump PM finds one of two 10kW strip banks open. The customer says "it heated fine last night." The correct framing is:

choices.text: Repair now: the dead bank means half the auxiliary/emergency capacity, which will be missed during defrost and the first deep cold
Disable the other bank to match

explanation: Mild-weather comfort hides missing aux capacity. The shortfall appears at the worst moment — defrost cycles and design-cold nights. Fix it found, not failed.

questionText: HVAC PM runs seasonally because:

choices.text: Cooling must be verified before summer and combustion safety before winter — matching failure seasons

explanation: Two visits bracket the two demand seasons — and the two failure rushes.

questionText: The spring PM's most failure-preventing electrical measurement is:

choices.text: The run capacitor value against its rating

explanation: Capacitors drift toward summer failure; measuring catches them for dollars before the heat-wave stranding.

questionText: Testing the condensate float switch in spring prevents:

choices.text: Summer ceiling/water damage from a clogged drain going unprotected

explanation: The float is the flood insurance; a PM that does not prove it works has not protected the home.

questionText: Gauges are connected during PM:

choices.text: Only when non-invasive readings (splits, amps, temps) disagree with health

explanation: The walkaround rule: every connection costs charge and risk; the numbers usually speak without it.

questionText: Recording this year's amps and splits matters because:

choices.text: Next year's comparison reveals drift before failure

explanation: Trend beats snapshot: recorded baselines turn PM into prediction.

questionText: The fall visit centers on:

choices.text: Combustion safety: heat exchanger, flame proving, draft, gas integrity, safeties, and CO measurement

explanation: Heating PM is the annual combustion-safety audit before the family lives with the fire all winter.

questionText: Proactively cleaning the flame sensor each fall prevents:
explanation: The most common furnace failure, prevented by the cheapest maintenance act in the trade.

questionText: Fall heat pump PM must verify:

choices.text: Defrost operation, reversing valve, auxiliary strip staging/amps, and crankcase heat

explanation: Winter-mode functions cannot be assumed from summer performance — exercise and measure each one.

questionText: Maintenance agreements benefit the service company by:

choices.text: Smoothing seasonal revenue, guaranteeing workload, building loyalty, and feeding documented repair pipelines

explanation: The agreement is the business engine; the tech's thorough, documented visits are its fuel.

questionText: Exercised safeties (limits, rollouts) during PM are:

choices.text: Verified functional per procedure and never bypassed

explanation: The kitchen rule forever: safeties are witnesses and guardians — proven, never silenced.

questionText: No-cool call: the indoor blower runs, but the outdoor unit is silent. Y reads 24V at the thermostat but 0V at the condenser contactor coil, and the air handler sits in a pan with a float switch. The most probable finding is:

choices.text: The condensate float switch has opened the Y circuit — check the drain pan before anything else

explanation: The float interrupts Y precisely to create this symptom instead of a ceiling stain. The 24V-present-here, absent-there measurement walks you straight to it.

questionText: A system cools weakly; suction pressure is low. Before adding refrigerant, the capstone rule demands:

choices.text: Verifying airflow (filter, blower, coil, ducts) — low airflow mimics low charge on the gauges

explanation: A starved evaporator reads low-suction whether the starvation is refrigerant or AIR. Charging an airflow problem overcharges the system the moment airflow is restored.

questionText: On a 104°F record afternoon (local design temp 96°F), a healthy, correctly charged system holds the house at 79°F against a 74°F setpoint, running continuously. The correct customer conversation is:

choices.text: The system has failed and needs replacement
The system is performing at design: extreme-day shortfall is a load/design reality — options include shading, envelope, or capacity additions, in writing
Add refrigerant for the heat wave

explanation: Equipment sized to design conditions falls behind beyond them — by design. Honest explanation plus options beats a false condemnation or a needless "repair."

questionText: Since Tuesday: three RTUs on one building log random board resets, and the VFD faults undervoltage each afternoon. The productive first question is:

choices.text: What do they share — and what changed Tuesday? (Utility work, a failing phase, new load on the service)
Which brand of board fails most?

explanation: Shared-cause reasoning: one sagging supply leg explains all four "failures." The victims' common denominator outranks any individual diagnosis.

questionText: The first checks on a silent outdoor unit are:

choices.text: Thermostat call, then 24V at the contactor coil — walking the control chain

explanation: Control before power before refrigerant: most silent condensers are control-chain finds.

questionText: A tripped condensate float switch presents as:

choices.text: No-cooling with the blower often still running — Y interrupted by design

explanation: The float kills cooling to prevent the flood; it is the no-cool call's first cheap answer.

questionText: Furnace no-heat diagnosis follows:

choices.text: The sequence of operation to its stall point, guided by the board code

explanation: Module 17's map: the failed step names the suspects; watching one full attempt localizes nearly everything.

questionText: "Air before refrigerant" exists because:

choices.text: Airflow faults mimic charge faults on gauges, and charging an airflow problem mischarges the system

explanation: Low airflow reads as low suction; the added gas becomes overcharge when the filter is finally changed.

questionText: Intermittent electronic faults are cracked by:

choices.text: Error histories plus correlating conditions (time, weather, load) with one-variable discipline

explanation: The flight-recorder habit: histories and patterns convert ghosts into schedules.

questionText: A hot back bedroom with healthy equipment is usually:

choices.text: A distribution/system issue: branch airflow, return path, envelope load

explanation: Comfort complaints with healthy equipment are Module 14/13 system stories, answered with measurement and options.

questionText: Extreme-weather "cannot keep up" on a design-sized system is:

choices.text: Design reality — capacity is sized to design conditions, and beyond them continuous running with indoor drift is expected

explanation: Design conditions bound the promise; the honest conversation covers load options, not false repairs.

questionText: Simultaneous odd behavior across all rooftop equipment suggests first:

choices.text: A shared cause: power quality, BAS command, or a common utility/service change

explanation: The kitchen's shared-cause law: what do the victims share, and what changed at onset?

questionText: HVAC repair-vs-replace framing adds:

choices.text: Efficiency deltas and refrigerant-platform clocks (R-22 dead, R-410A phasing) to age, history, and downtime

explanation: Energy savings and refrigerant futures are real money — honest numbers, customer decision.

questionText: A repair is verified by:

choices.text: Real-load operation observed: full pull-down, complete heat cycle, defrost as applicable

explanation: "Runs" is not "works": the machine does its actual job, measured, before the truck leaves.

questionText: The certification path that most directly parallels the kitchen trade's CFESA credential is:

choices.text: NATE — the industry's recognized knowledge certification with core and specialty exams

explanation: NATE is HVAC's industry credential ladder: Core plus specialties, employer-recognized, and typically employer-funded once you are producing.

questionText: Manufacturer training schools matter economically because:

choices.text: Warranty authorization makes you dispatchable and billable on that brand — and VRF work is gated behind them

explanation: The kitchen-course lesson identically: OEM authorization is how service companies win warranty work, and how techs become the ones sent to the good equipment.

questionText: The most frequently replaced part in residential HVAC — and therefore the van-stock priority — is:

choices.text: Run capacitors in the common sizes

explanation: The dual run capacitor is the trade's bread-and-butter failure: stock the sizes, test against ratings, and carry a universal for the odd one.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

subcategory: The Kit, the Craft, and the Paths
questionText: The strongest long-term career asset in residential HVAC service is:

choices.text: A reputation for honest diagnosis and framing — homeowners remember who told them the truth

explanation: Replacement-pressure shops exist, but reputation compounds: the honest tech's referrals, reviews, and eventual customer list are the real equity.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: The HVAC trade's labor outlook is:

choices.text: Chronic shortage with expanding scope (heat pumps, A2L transition, electrification)

explanation: Retirements outrun entrants while the work itself grows — the strongest shortage story of the three trades.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: The legal prerequisite for refrigerant work is:

choices.text: EPA Section 608 certification (Universal as the standard target)

explanation: 608 is federal law; everything else is professional credential on top of it.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: NATE certification is:

choices.text: The industry's recognized knowledge credential: Core plus specialty exams

explanation: The HVAC analog of CFESA: employer-recognized, specialty-structured, usually employer-funded.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: Light-commercial HVAC work centers on:

choices.text: Packaged rooftop units serving restaurants, retail, and offices

explanation: RTU country — and the same buildings whose kitchens the sister course serves.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: Entry-level HVAC compensation typically starts around:

choices.text: $40-55K, rising to $60-85K with experience and beyond for specialists

explanation: The shortage keeps floors rising; overtime rides every heat wave and cold snap.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: The air-side instruments the curriculum demands are:

choices.text: A digital psychrometer and a manometer for static pressure

explanation: Modules 13-14 in hardware: WB/DB/RH plus TESP are the airflow diagnosis kit.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: A2L refrigerant adoption affects the toolkit by requiring:

choices.text: A2L-rated recovery machines, hoses, and leak detection as fleets transition

explanation: The mildly flammable class carries equipment ratings — the transition is a tooling event too.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: Van stock should be organized around:

choices.text: The trade's failure patterns: capacitors, contactors, ignition/flame parts, condensate protection

explanation: Stock the priors: the modules' failure catalog is the packing list.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: The controls/BAS specialty path builds on:

choices.text: Module 21 literacy: DDC architecture, sensor truth, and VFDs

explanation: Commercial buildings run on controls; the tech who reads them writes their own ticket.
referenceBookSection: Module 25 — Career in HVAC Field Service

questionText: The common foundation of every path — lead, specialist, manager, owner — is:

choices.text: Honest diagnosis, faithful documentation, and continuous learning

explanation: Three courses, one portal, one answer: the habits are the career.
